task.goal: Design a way to detect overnight water leaks in an older apartment block without replacing meters.
hard_constraints: Caretaker can inspect existing daily meter readings and common-area pipes for five mornings; no new sensors.
Do not shut off occupied apartments or disclose unit-level consumption.
Distinguish real leaks from delayed meter entry and shared cleaning use; specify a confirmation and rollback check.
task.available_resources: Paper meter log and building maintenance roster.
task.expected_result: A feasible detection and response workflow.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Timestamp-corrected building water balance with a cleaning comparison
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: identify persistent unexplained building-level consumption after correcting recording delays and separating scheduled cleaning. This changes the decision from reacting to a large daily entry to checking whether actual, comparable meter intervals remain unusually high.

For five mornings, the caretaker copies the existing cumulative building reading, actual observation time, paper-entry time, and any known missed reading. Calculate consumption between actual observations; combine intervals spanning a missed reading rather than assigning the catch-up amount to one day. Use only building totals. If the log contains only unit readings, retain those privately and report aggregates only; without sufficiently complete readings, mark the calculation inconclusive.

Use the maintenance roster to identify cleaning periods and other known shared water use. Where operationally convenient, schedule ordinary cleaning after the morning reading and include at least two intervals without water-based cleaning. Do not restrict residents’ use. Compare these intervals with comparable historical intervals already in the paper log, if available, and with the cleaning intervals. A continuing excess during cleaning-free intervals is a reason to inspect accessible common pipes, joints, tanks, and drains for corroboration.

Needs are the existing log, roster, and caretaker time. The method assumes readings cover a consistent building boundary and that shared activities can be identified. Daily totals cannot establish that a leak occurred specifically overnight, and variable resident use can mimic an excess. Treat unexplained totals as a screening signal, not proof or grounds for apartment intervention.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Small check: compare conclusions from raw daily log entries with conclusions from timestamp-corrected intervals. An apparent spike that disappears when a delayed entry is spread over its actual interval falsifies that leak alert. Excess that occurs only with cleaning supports shared use instead. Confirm a suspected leak through a visible active defect or qualified maintenance inspection, without shutting off occupied apartments. After an authorized repair, compare the next available comparable reading and inspect the repair. If consumption stays high, roll back the claim that this defect explains the excess and reopen investigation; if the repair seeps, arrange corrective maintenance. Five mornings may yield only an inconclusive screen.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repeated physical tracing of common-area wetness
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: detect an active common-pipe leak by repeated observations of where fresh water originates, using meter records to check timing explanations rather than making consumption the primary detector. This can find a small visible leak even when residents’ variable use obscures it in daily totals.

On the first morning, establish a short repeatable route along accessible common-area pipes, joints, valves, tank overflows, and nearby floor or wall surfaces. Record locations and whether each is dry, damp, dripping, or visibly flowing on paper. Inspect before scheduled cleaning on each of the five mornings. Ask the caretaker to record any cleaning completed since the previous inspection, using the maintenance roster; where practical, move cleaning on the route until after inspection. Do not enter apartments, operate apartment valves, or inspect unsafe or inaccessible spaces.

For a suspect location, observe whether fresh water visibly emerges from a joint or overflow. If normal maintenance practice permits, wipe an accessible surface dry with an existing cleaning cloth and inspect again before cleaning begins. Record moisture returning at its source separately from residual floor wetness. Condensation, rain ingress, and cleaning splash remain alternative explanations unless a source is traceable.

Needs are caretaker time, paper notes, access to existing common pipes, and ordinary cleaning supplies if already available. No instrumentation or new sensors are required. The approach assumes a leak leaves an accessible physical sign; concealed leaks and silent underground losses can escape detection. A morning finding establishes an active defect, but does not establish that it ran all night. Existing meter entries can indicate whether building consumption also remains elevated, after accounting for delayed entries.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Small check: compare one suspect joint with a nearby unaffected surface under the same conditions. Reappearance directly from the joint before cleaning supports leakage; comparable diffuse moisture on both surfaces weakens that explanation and suggests condensation or another source. Confirm through direct source observation or maintenance inspection, recording uncertainty if the origin remains hidden. Arrange only repairs that preserve occupied-apartment supply. Reinspect the repaired site on the next available morning and review the correctly timed aggregate meter interval. Recurring moisture triggers corrective inspection; unchanged building consumption rolls back any claim that the repaired defect explained the building’s excess. Dry accessible pipes do not clear concealed plumbing.

EXPAND.title: Temporarily isolate a verified common-use branch
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: remove pressure from one dedicated common-area branch and observe whether unexplained building consumption falls. This tests a concealed loss on that branch even when no wet surface is visible.

On morning one, the caretaker checks the maintenance roster and accessible plumbing for an existing valve serving only a cleaning tap or other nonessential common outlet. Proceed only if its service boundary is established and closing it cannot interrupt apartments, fire protection, essential equipment, or hygiene facilities. If these conditions cannot be established, this route is inapplicable.

Use mornings one and two as the baseline interval. After the second reading, an authorized caretaker closes the verified branch valve and records its position and closure time. Keep it closed through morning four, with affected cleaning deferred and recorded. Inspect accessible downstream pipes each morning. Use existing daily building readings, recording actual observation times and distinguishing delayed transcription from delayed observation; compare consumption over actual intervals. Do not attribute a catch-up entry to a single day. Keep all reporting at building level.

A repeated reduction during isolation identifies the branch as a maintenance lead, not proof: removing legitimate common use and changing resident demand can also reduce totals. Confirmation requires maintenance to identify an actual defect on that branch. Repair only where apartment supply can remain available.

Needs are the existing log, roster, a verified dedicated valve, and authority to operate it. Compared with corrected totals and routine visual inspection, the added causal intervention may reveal an otherwise concealed branch leak. Its limits are uncertain valve boundaries, incomplete isolation, variable household demand, and loss of common-service availability. Daily readings still cannot establish that leakage occurred specifically overnight.
EXPAND.experiment: Owner: caretaker, for five mornings. Compare the isolated intervals with the baseline and with the simpler timestamp-corrected consumption screen. Record both detection evidence and deferred cleaning or service disruption. Stop immediately if valve operation affects an unexpected service; restore its original position when safe and hand off. If isolation adds no interpretable evidence, abandon the trial. After a confirmed repair, restore the branch and inspect it on morning five if timing permits; otherwise explicitly hand off follow-up. Recurring leakage requires corrective maintenance. A consumption rebound without legitimate common use rolls back the claim of resolution; unchanged totals roll back any claim that this branch explained the building excess.

EXPAND.title: Reconcile an existing master meter against existing downstream totals
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: use conservation across nested meter boundaries to separate water lost in shared distribution from water delivered to apartments. Household overnight use appears in downstream totals; leakage between the master meter and downstream meters can appear as a persistent residual.

This route applies only if the existing paper log already contains a building master reading and sufficiently complete downstream readings covering the same supply. It requires no replacement meters or additional reading rounds. On morning one, the caretaker establishes the boundaries from available records and accessible common pipes. Identify common outlets supplied outside the downstream meters. If coverage or boundaries cannot be established, stop this route as inconclusive.

For five mornings, calculate master consumption minus the sum of downstream consumption over matching actual observation intervals. Use cumulative differences across a longer common interval when entries were delayed; do not compare amounts merely sharing a paper entry date. Where observation times differ materially and matching endpoints are unavailable, do not interpret the residual.

Consult the maintenance roster for unmetered cleaning use. Seek repeated residuals during intervals without that use, rather than subtracting an invented cleaning allowance. Inspect common distribution pipes along the unmatched supply path and hand a persistent unexplained residual to maintenance for confirmation. Keep unit readings within authorized caretaker access and disclose only the residual and building-level findings.

Needs are existing nested readings, reliable boundary information, and caretaker calculation time. Compared with a building-total screen, this can discount changing resident demand and direct inspection upstream of apartment meters. Meter inaccuracies, storage changes, omitted outlets, and mismatched times can imitate leakage. It cannot detect a leak downstream of an apartment meter or prove overnight timing.
EXPAND.experiment: Owner: caretaker, with a five-morning stop rule. First reconcile one interval with complete, matching endpoints; stop if those prerequisites fail. Compare the residual-based alert with the simpler corrected building-total alert, recording calculation time and unresolved boundary uncertainty. No useful residual separation means no demonstrated improvement. Confirm a suspected loss through an identified active defect or qualified maintenance inspection, preserving apartment supply. After an authorized repair, inspect the site and repeat the matched reconciliation when readings become available. A persistent residual withdraws the claim that the repair explains the loss; renewed wetness triggers corrective maintenance. If confirmation or follow-up exceeds five mornings, hand off the dated records and leave the case unresolved.

EXPAND.title: Upgrade of P0: corrected building totals with a mandatory confirmation gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: screen for persistent unexplained building consumption using comparable observation intervals, then require physical confirmation before treating the signal as a leak. The substantive fix to P0 is an explicit boundary between a suspicious total and an actionable defect, with a fallback when timestamps or cleaning records are inadequate.

The caretaker owns a five-morning trial. Record the existing cumulative building reading, actual observation time, entry time, and cleaning since the previous observation. Separate late transcription from a missed observation: combine intervals across missing observations instead of assigning accumulated consumption to the entry date. Use building totals only; disclose no unit readings.

Use the roster to arrange two intervals without water-based common cleaning, provided ordinary cleaning can be rescheduled without compromising hygiene or adding overtime. Record displaced work. Compare corrected consumption with comparable historical intervals if the paper log contains them. Without a credible baseline, five readings support only a tentative pattern, not a numerical leak threshold.

Repeated unexplained excess triggers inspection of accessible common pipes before cleaning. Confirm only when fresh water can be traced to a defective joint, outlet, or overflow; otherwise hand maintenance an unresolved building-level anomaly. No apartment shutoff is permitted. If interval alignment or cleaning attribution fails, abandon the numerical diagnosis and use the five morning pipe inspections instead.

Needs are the log, roster, caretaker time, and accessible pipework. Resident demand can mimic excess; daily readings cannot establish overnight timing. After a repair that preserves apartment supply, check both the physical source and the next comparable existing reading. If evidence disappears after correcting entries or recording cleaning, withdraw the leak flag and restore the normal cleaning schedule.
EXPAND.experiment: On morning five, compare flags from raw daily entries with flags from corrected intervals and inspection. Count confirmed sources, unresolved flags, caretaker minutes, and displaced cleaning. Stop schedule changes if hygiene or staffing suffers. If correction adds work without resolving any suspected leak or false alarm, retain simple morning inspection and report the quantitative screen as inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: Upgrade of P1: source recurrence with an explicit false-wetness and recovery check
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: confirm leakage through fresh water repeatedly emerging from an identifiable common-pipe source. Preserve P1’s short visual route, but add a decision gate that prevents residual cleaning water, condensation, or rain from becoming an unsupported repair request.

For five mornings, the caretaker follows the same accessible route before cleaning, noting dry surfaces, dampness, active drops, and the apparent origin. Use the maintenance roster to record cleaning that occurred since the previous visit. Keep resident consumption private and leave apartment valves untouched. Do not touch hot pipes, electrical hazards, or unsafe surfaces.

At a suspect accessible joint, first inspect the surfaces above it: water tracking downward does not establish that the joint leaks. If an existing cleaning cloth is available, dry the exterior and revisit later during the same morning inspection period, before cleaning. Otherwise observe directly for a newly forming drop. Repeat on another morning when practical. Confirmation requires visible emergence from the fitting or outlet; dampness alone remains unresolved. Record competing explanations such as widespread condensation or rain-related wetness.

Use existing meter entries only as supporting context, correcting delayed entries and identifying shared cleaning. A catch-up entry cannot confirm the physical finding. If no source is accessible, hand maintenance the location and uncertainty rather than extending the search into apartments.

Needs are caretaker time, paper notes, accessible pipes, and optionally an already available cloth. Concealed or intermittent leaks can be missed, and morning observations cannot prove all-night operation. Request repair through the roster only where apartment supply can remain available; otherwise hand off for a compliant plan. Reinspect after repair. If recurrence identifies another source, reopen the finding; if cleaning explains the wetness, withdraw it and resume the usual schedule.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare an initial wetness-only list with the source-confirmed list after five mornings. Record confirmed active sources, unresolved locations, extra inspection minutes, and cleaning delays. Stop wiping or revisits where access is unsafe or cleaning would be compromised. No confirmed sources after repeated checks means this trial has not demonstrated detection benefit; it does not establish that the building is leak-free.

EXPAND.title: Unaided listening to locate concealed common-pipe flow
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: use persistent audible flow, hissing, or repeated refill sounds to locate a concealed common-system fault that leaves no visible wet patch. Listening provides a different detection channel from meter arithmetic or surface wetness; it remains a screening method because normal household demand can sound similar.

The caretaker selects a short route through safely accessible common pipe locations on morning one. During each of five morning rounds, pause at the same locations and record whether sound is absent, intermittent, or continuous during a brief observation. Listen without contacting pipes, opening equipment, entering apartments, or installing instruments. Record only common-system locations, never inferred household activity.

Use the maintenance roster to identify cleaning times. Where convenient, listen before cleaning starts, then revisit a suspect location later that morning after the known shared activity has ended. Do not ask residents to stop using water. A sound disappearing with cleaning is explained shared use; repeated sound outside cleaning periods is a maintenance lead, not proof of leakage. Correct delayed meter entries before treating building consumption as supporting evidence.

For a localized lead, inspect nearby accessible joints, overflows, and common outlets. Confirmation requires finding an actual escaping-water source or maintenance identifying a defect while preserving apartment supply. Do not operate an uncertain valve to test the sound. If sound remains unlocalized or could be ordinary demand, close the five-day trial as unresolved and hand over the observations without a leak declaration.

Needs are caretaker hearing, paper notes, the roster, and quiet enough access. Some real leaks are silent; pumps and resident demand can mask or imitate them. After any compliant repair, repeat the same listening and physical inspection. Persistent sound means the acoustic explanation must be reconsidered, not that further repairs are automatically justified. Restore any deferred cleaning and withdraw unsupported flags.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare leads found by listening with those found by the ordinary visual route during the same five mornings. Record any independently confirmed defect found only through sound, additional minutes, and unnecessary maintenance referrals. Stop if listening causes access risks or material cleaning delays. If it produces only ambiguous sounds and no confirmed additional source, the trial shows no demonstrated gain over visual inspection.
